- Not searched, from memory [M]: Bazerman and Neale, *Negotiating Rationally* (Free Press, 1992; older); Bazerman and Moore, *Judgment in Managerial Decision Making* (Wiley, 9th ed. believed, verify); Shell, *Bargaining for Advantage* (Penguin, 2nd ed. 2006, a 3rd ed. may exist; verify); Thompson (ed.) *Handbook of Negotiation Research* / Bazerman et al. "Negotiation" (Annual Review of Psychology, 2000) as a short literature review; Brett, *Negotiating Globally* (Jossey-Bass, 3rd ed. 2014); Sebenius, Lax, Raiffa, *Negotiation Analysis* (Raiffa, Richardson, Metcalfe, *Negotiation Analysis: The Science and Art of Collaborative Decision Making*, Harvard UP 2002) is the most formal, decision/game-theory treatment and arguably the most relevant to a quantitative agent.

### Inferences
- For a scored multi-issue agent, the most directly useful research-based works are Raiffa et al. *Negotiation Analysis* (formal, utility and trade-off modelling), Thompson (evidence on integrative tactics, e.g. multi-issue offers and logrolling), and Lewicki (broad textbook, standard syllabus text). Getting to Yes and Shell are frameworks, not tested prescriptions.
- Lewicki 8th and Thompson 7th are both 2020 editions; as of Oct 2026 I did not confirm newer editions. Check publisher sites before citing.

### Gaps
- No Google Scholar counts were retrievable; reputation signals above are memory only. A follow-up fetch of Scholar or Semantic Scholar per title is needed.
- Editions of Shell, Bazerman and Moore, Raiffa et al., and Brett not verified here.
- Monthly status of the Getting to Yes 30th-anniversary edition unknown.

## Which procurement/supply-management textbooks cover supplier negotiation?

### Takeaway
Verified current editions: van Weele and Rozemeijer, *Procurement and Supply Chain Management*, 8th ed. (Cengage, 2022); Handfield, Giunipero, Monczka, Patterson, *Purchasing and Supply Chain Management*, 8th ed. (Cengage, copyright 2026). Chopra's 7th ed. is 2018/2019 and covers sourcing/pricing but little negotiation tactics.

### Cited Findings
- van Weele and Rozemeijer, *Procurement and Supply Chain Management*, 8th ed., Cengage, 2022, ISBN 9781473779112; adds "Theory snapshots". NOT Springer (earlier editions titled *Purchasing and Supply Chain Management*, Cengage, 5th ed. 2010) — [Cengage UK](https://www.cengage.uk/c/procurement-and-supply-chain-management-8e-van-weele-rozemeijer/9781473779112). [V]
- Handfield, Giunipero, Monczka, Patterson, *Purchasing and Supply Chain Management*, 8th ed., Cengage; hardback ISBN 9798214042039, eBook 9798214042084; copyright 2026, availability April 2025 (dates vary by site); new coverage of AI in procurement, resilience, counterfeit mitigation; 7th ed. was 2021 — [Cengage](https://cengage.com/c/purchasing-and-supply-chain-management-8e-handfield-giunipero-monczka-patterson/9798214042039). [V]
- Chopra, *Supply Chain Management: Strategy, Planning, and Operation*, 7th ed., Pearson, 2018 (© 2019), ISBN 9780134731889; Global Edition 2020. Co-author Meindl credited on earlier editions; not confirmed for 7th. Covers sourcing, pricing, facilities, inventory — [Pearson](https://www.pearson.com/store/en-us/p/supply-chain-management-strategy-planning-and-operation/P200000005863). [V]
- Not verified here [M]: Kraljic (1983) "Purchasing must become supply management", *Harvard Business Review* (the original article, a short read, not a book); Gelderman and van Weele on Kraljic-matrix applications (journal papers, *J. Purchasing & Supply Management*); Cousins, Lamming, Lawson, Squire, *Strategic Supply Management: Principles, Theories and Practice* (FT Prentice Hall, 2008); Lysons and Farrington, *Procurement and Supply Chain Management* (Pearson, 9th ed. believed, verify); Cox's power-regime and Schuh et al., *The Purchasing Value Chain* are other cites. Procurement-specific negotiation texts such as Reck and Long, or Kolb and Williams, not researched.

### Inferences
- Procurement textbooks give the business context (total cost of ownership, payment terms, contract length, supplier segmentation) that maps directly to the term-sheet issues; they are weaker than the negotiation canon on tactics and evidence.
- The Kraljic matrix literature supports adapting strategy to supplier leverage: bottleneck and strategic items warrant more cooperative, longer-contract deals; leverage items warrant more competitive stances. This is [M]-level reasoning.

### Gaps
- Kraljic, Cousins et al., Lysons and Farrington not searched; no citation counts or reviews found.
- No Journal of Purchasing and Supply Management book reviews found.

## Which popular books are practitioner opinion with weaker evidence, and how do experts rate them?

### Takeaway
Voss (*Never Split the Difference*) is practitioner opinion built on hostage-negotiation experience; I found no systematic academic evaluation. Treat tactics (labels, calibrated questions, "no"-oriented questions) as hypotheses, not tested findings. Getting to Yes and Shell are influential but also framework/practitioner books.

### Cited Findings
- Reviews note that Voss's fairness claims are not put in the context of the academic literature, and that he says where field experience and academic advice conflicted he sided with experience — [Gorelik review](https://gorelik.net/2020/04/25/book-review-never-split-the-difference-by-chris-voss), [SQL Server Central review](https://www.sqlservercentral.com/blogs/bks-bookshelf-never-split-the-difference). Blog-level sources; weak.
- Inside Higher Ed frames the book's message as most conventional advice being wrong; opinion, not evidence — [Inside Higher Ed](https://www.insidehighered.com/node/11954).
- Several search hits claiming the book is "significant empirical scholarship" were templated filler and disregarded.
- Voss, Raz, *Never Split the Difference*, Harper Business, 2016. [M]. It is a bestseller; academic negotiation scholars commonly view it as engaging but not research-based [M, unverified].
- Fisher/Ury/Patton and Shell: widely adopted (Harvard PON, Program on Negotiation, associated with the Harvard Negotiation Project) but criticised by scholars for limited empirical testing and for underplaying distributive bargaining [M].

### Inferences
- For a bot-vs-bot, scored setting, popular emotional tactics (mirroring, labels) have little direct value; the numeric principles (anchoring, concession patterns, BATNA, trade-offs across issues) matter more.

### Gaps
- No peer-reviewed or Negotiation Journal review of Voss found; a targeted search of *Negotiation Journal* is needed.

## Which are available via the TUM library or open access?

### Takeaway
TUM runs a catalogue at search.ub.tum.de (VuFind) and offers 300,000+ e-books incl. about 70,000 Springer titles via eAccess; I found no evidence of Oxford/Cambridge e-book packages. I could not verify holdings for any individual title.

### Cited Findings
- TUM University Library licensed Springer Book Archives subject areas, giving about 70,000 Springer eBooks (2015 news item); other page says over 300,000 scientific e-books — [UB TUM news](https://ub.tum.de/en/news?page=105), [UB TUM](https://www.ub.tum.de/en/node/5558). Dated; recheck.
- Access is via TUM ID (eAccess); licence terms forbid systematic downloading — [UB TUM](https://www.ub.tum.de/en/node/5558).
- Oxford University Press mentioned only for e-journals since January 2024; Wiley, Sage, T&F as e-journals — [UB TUM](https://www.ub.tum.de/en/node/5558).
- The TUM catalogue does index at least the Elgar *Research Handbook on Gender and Negotiation* (a record exists at [search.ub.tum.de](https://search.ub.tum.de/vufind/Record/DE-604.BV047089845?lng=en)); this shows the catalogue is searchable but not that it holds the other titles.
- Elgar offers the Olekalns/Adair handbook as eBook for purchase — [Elgar](https://www.e-elgar.com/shop/handbook-of-research-on-negotiation).
- Pearson offers an eTextbook (subscription/rental, DRM-locked platform) for Thompson; Cengage sells eTextbook for Handfield et al. — links above. DRM status presumed [M].

### Inferences
- Springer-published titles (none of the headline books above) would be most likely to be free via TUM. Most listed books are from Pearson, Cengage, McGraw-Hill, Penguin, HBR Press: expect physical library loan (search.ub.tum.de, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek) or purchase. Check via TUM catalogue before buying.
- No open-access full text of the main textbooks found; none should be sought via unauthorised copies.

### Gaps
- Per-title TUM holdings unchecked (catalogue search not executed); Primo use at TUM unconfirmed (TUM appears to use VuFind/OPAC).
- Oxford/Cambridge e-book access at TUM unconfirmed.

# Core experimental findings on bargaining behaviour (for an e-mail buyer agent with multi-issue term sheets)

Method note: web research only (about 15 search/fetch calls), no Tacto API. Everything below comes from search-result abstracts and publisher/repository pages. I read NO full texts. "Access" is my guess unless stated. Items marked [UNVERIFIED] came from my memory or a single secondary page and need a DOI check. Nearly all studies are lab or online experiments with students or panel participants, not field data.

## 1. First offers and anchoring

### Takeaway
The first-offer effect is large and robust in simple, single-issue, price-type bargaining, and it holds across power, culture and multi-issue settings. Its costs are impasse risk and lower benefit as complexity rises. Extreme offers anchor but can offend and cause walk-aways, especially from low-power recipients. Effect sizes come from one 2025 meta-analysis and are not final-paper verified.

### Cited Findings
- Meta-analysis of 90 studies (Petrowsky, Loschelder et al., OBHDP 2025, preregistered, robust variance estimation) plus experiments (Studies 2a-2b, N = 2,121). Making the first offer gives an advantage and ambitious first offers give economic gains, but ambitious offers raise impasse odds. Effects shrink as the number and type of issues increase, and the mechanisms change. Conference abstract values: first-mover g = 0.49, first-offer magnitude g = 1.30, offer-outcome r = 0.53 (pre-publication figures, check against the final paper). Heterogeneity is high. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2025.104448. Access: the journal is paywalled, but a Leuphana PubData parallel publication (DOI 10.48548/pubdata-3207) appears open access. Abstract level only. — [Leuphana PubData](https://pubdata.leuphana.de/entities/publication/29dc7e5d-01eb-420a-b73d-66e0be7cd440); [FIS Leuphana summary](https://fis.leuphana.de/en/publications/the-power-and-peril-of-first-offers-in-negotiations-a-conceptual-/)
- Galinsky & Mussweiler (2001), JPSP 81(4), 657-669. Three lab experiments: first offers anchor outcomes, and the effect is reduced when the counterpart takes perspective or focuses on their own target/BATNA information. DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.81.4.657 [UNVERIFIED, from memory]. APA/library access (TUM). Abstract only. — [Kellogg record](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/2001/first-offers-as-anchors-the-role-of-perspective-taking)
- Orr & Guthrie (2006), Ohio State J. on Dispute Resolution 21, 597; meta-analysis of simulated negotiations. Anchoring has a significant effect on deals, tested against experience and information environment. A secondary blog gives r about 0.50 (0.37 adjusted for experience); verify before use. Open access on bepress. Abstract only. — [bepress](https://works.bepress.com/chris-guthrie/18); [Vanderbilt IR](https://ir.vanderbilt.edu/handle/1803/7415); secondary: [Miles Mediation](https://milesmediation.com/blog/make-the-first-move-and-drop-the-anchor-miles-mediation/)
- Gunia, Swaab, Sivanathan & Galinsky (2013), PSPB 39, 1547-1558, "Remarkable robustness of the first-offer effect: across culture, power, and issues". The effect held across cultures and in multi-issue negotiations, and low-power negotiators gained from moving first. The first offer works through the distributive issues, not the integrative or compatible ones. DOI not retrieved. Abstract only. Lab. — [LBS record](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/t/the-remarkable-robustness-of-the-first-offer-effect-across-culture-power-and-issues)
- Extreme offers: Schweinsberg, Ku, Wang & Pillutla (2012), JESP 48(1), 226-231, "Starting high and ending with nothing". Two experiments. Extreme first offers still anchor counteroffers and outcomes, but they offend recipients and risk impasse. Low-power and high-power recipients were equally offended, but low-power ones walked away. Abstract only. (A search note said the Kellogg subtitle differs; I did not check author order or the DOI.) — [LBS](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/s/starting-high-and-ending-with-nothing-the-role-of-anchors-and-power-in-negotiations); [ISB](https://eprints.exchange.isb.edu/id/eprint/1559/)
- Precision: Loschelder, Friese & Trötschel (2017), JESP 70, 164-176, three experiments. Precise anchors (e.g. 4,970 vs 5,000) anchor recipients more strongly, via an attribution of competence. Senders who use precise numbers choose less extreme (less ambitious) offers. Abstract level only; no effect sizes retrieved. — [Saarland repository](https://publikationen.sulb.uni-saarland.de/handle/20.500.11880/27829); [PON summary](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/dealmaking-daily/negotiation-research-can-use-effective-first-offer-strive-precision-nb/?amp)
- Mussweiler & Strack (1999), JESP 35, 136-164, is the selective accessibility account of anchoring (anchor-consistent knowledge becomes more accessible). Harris et al. (2019) report failures to replicate a key result of that theory (UCL preprint; not read). I did not find a direct Many Labs anchoring replication via search; my memory says Many Labs 1 replicated classic anchoring, but this is unverified. — [LBS record](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/a/anchoring-accessibility-as-a-cause-of-judgmental-assimilation); [UCL](https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10074759/1/HarrisEtAl_2019_anchoring.pdf)
- Brooks & Schweitzer (2011), OBHDP 115, 43-54: incidental anxiety lowered expectations and opening offers and worsened outcomes (four studies; HBS summary says $6.60 vs $7.94 in one study). Relevant only as evidence that low aspirations lower first offers. — [IDEAS](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v115y2011i1p43-54.html); [HBS](https://hbswk.hbs.edu/item/overcoming-nervous-nelly)

### Inferences
- For a buyer agent, anchor first with an ambitious but defensible opening, and keep it believable; reserve extreme offers for situations where walking away is not costly. This is an inference from Petrowsky, Schweinsberg and the Leonardelli entries below.
- With a precise (non-round) opening figure, the recipient may be anchored more strongly, but the agent should not shrink its ambition because of it. This is my inference from Loschelder et al.
- In a multi-issue term sheet the anchor effect is concentrated in the price (distributive) issue (Gunia 2013) and weakens as issues multiply (Petrowsky 2025).

### Gaps
- Final effect sizes, moderator tables and the exact impasse increase from Petrowsky 2025 were not read.
- No direct evidence on anchoring in e-mail or LLM-vs-LLM negotiation was found.
- Replication status of the negotiation-specific effects: no failed replication of the first-offer effect found; the replication of the cognitive mechanism is contested (Harris 2019).

## 2. Concession patterns

### Takeaway
Hard bargaining wins more money but costs relationship and, in some conditions, impasses. Reciprocating concessions is the best soft strategy. Shrinking concession steps signal a nearing limit and make recipients less ambitious; the evidence is a single 2021 lab paper plus older work.

### Cited Findings
- Hüffmeier, Freund, Zerres, Backhaus & Hertel (2014), J. Management 40(3), 866-892. Meta-analysis of 34 studies of distributive negotiation (135 economic and 30 socioemotional effect sizes). Hardline strategies gave higher economic outcomes and softline gave higher socioemotional outcomes. Hardliners gained most with visual contact, knowledge of the bargaining zone and a maximize-own-outcome instruction. Softliners did best when they accurately reciprocated concessions, and softline did not win even when impasse risk and cost were high (contrary to prediction). DOI 10.1177/0149206311423788. Likely paywalled (TUM). Abstract only; no d/r values retrieved. — [UvA DARE](https://dare.uva.nl/id/801197e8-e374-4128-aeb3-c66c06cb8812)
- Tey, Schaerer, Madan & Swaab (2021), OBHDP 165, 153-166. Seven studies, N = 2,311. Decreasing concession sequences (e.g. 1,500, 1,210, 1,180, 1,170) lead recipients to make less ambitious counteroffers and reach worse deals, mediated by an inflated estimate of the counterpart's reservation price. The effect is strongest for moderate decline rates and for declines over more rounds; setting a target in advance partly protects recipients. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2021.05.003. Abstract only. Lab/online. — [INSEAD](https://www.insead.edu/faculty-research/publications/journal-articles/impact-concession-patterns-negotiations-when-and-why)
- Lawler & MacMurray (1980), a programmed-opponent study cited in a search snippet: the best response depended on the opponent's opening stance, and prior deadlock reduced concessions. Single secondary snippet, not verified. — [Leuphana snippet](https://fis.leuphana.de/en/publications/concession-patterns-in-dyadic-negotiations-empirically-contrastin/)
- A separate study (found via the same search, authors not retrieved) reports that distributive concession making raises impasse rates, driven by loss of conceded value and not by reciprocity-norm violation. — [TU Dortmund](https://eldorado.tu-dortmund.de/items/f909800c-1d5e-4cb0-9fa9-9745ab154670/full)

### Inferences
- A seller-facing buyer agent should avoid showing a clear shrinking-step pattern if it wants to hide its limit, and should expect a seller using one to be signalling a limit (but it may be a bluff).
- Reciprocate counterpart concessions in kind; start tough and concede on a pattern that does not leak the limit.

### Gaps
- No meta-analysis on concession timing found; no evidence tied specifically to e-mail asynchronous bargaining.
- Effect sizes of Hüffmeier 2014 not retrieved.

## 3. BATNA, reservation prices and power

### Takeaway
Better alternatives raise outcomes and the propensity to move first, but the first-offer anchor can outweigh BATNA effects and, per one study, having no BATNA can beat a weak one. Evidence on disclosing information is weak in my findings.

### Cited Findings
- Kim & Fragale (2005), J. Applied Psychology 90(2), 373-381. BATNA advantage mattered more when the bargaining zone was small, contribution advantage when it was large. DOI 10.1037/0021-9010.90.2.373 (as found by search; not opened). Abstract level. — [summary page](https://academicnewsletter.sufe.edu.cn/info/372348)
- Magee, Galinsky & Gruenfeld (2007), PSPB 33(2), 200-212. Five experiments. Higher power increased propensity to negotiate and to move first; negotiators with strong BATNAs were over three times as likely to intend to open (as reported by the abstract summary); making the first offer gave a bargaining edge. Abstract only. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/2007/power-propensity-to-negotiate-and-moving-first-in-competitive/?p=1)
- Pinkley, Neale & Bennett (1994), OBHDP 57(1), 97-116, "The impact of alternatives to settlement in dyadic negotiation". Content not retrieved; only the citation. A 1995 Pinkley OBHDP paper on BATNA knowledge was not confirmed. — [IDEAS](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v57y1994i1p97-116.html)
- Schaerer, Swaab & Galinsky, Psychological Science (about 2015; year and title unconfirmed): negotiators with no BATNA did better than those with weak BATNAs, because they made higher first offers (anchors weigh more than power). Seen only in a search note; [UNVERIFIED]. — [APS](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/minds-business/negotiating-with-nothing-holds-surprise-benefits.html)
- Schweinsberg et al. 2012 (section 1): power moderates whether extreme anchors lead to walk-aways.
- Gunia, Brett, Nandkeolyar & Kamdar (2011), J. Applied Psychology 96(4), 774-789, three studies: lower interpersonal trust in Indian negotiators went with less information-sharing and lower joint gains than for US negotiators. Relevant to information exchange, not BATNA. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/2011/paying-a-price-culture-trust-and-negotiation-consequences/?p=1)
- Kong, Dirks & Ferrin (2014), Acad. Management J. 57(5), 1235-1255. Meta-analysis of 38 independent studies on trust within negotiations, with three contingencies. Effect sizes not retrieved. — [MetaTOC](https://metatoc.com/papers/23303-interpersonal-trust-within-negotiations-meta-analytic-evidence-critical-contingencies-and-directions-for-future-research)

### Inferences
- A buyer agent should have its BATNA/reservation value internally and may move first when its BATNA is good, but should not reveal the reservation price (no direct evidence retrieved on disclosure; this is a design judgment). Evidence is largely lab.

### Gaps
- Evidence on disclosing versus hiding BATNA/reservation price (Pinkley 1995, Morris/Larrick/Su, Gunia et al. alternatives) was not retrieved. Treat as open.
- Replication status of the weak-BATNA result is unknown.

## 4. Multi-issue offers, MESOs, logrolling, questions, information

### Takeaway
MESOs, information exchange and question-asking raise joint gains and rapport in lab studies; the fixed-pie bias is the main obstacle. A buyer agent sending packages with several equivalent options should gain both anchoring and integrative benefits. The evidence is lab-based.

### Cited Findings
- Leonardelli, Gu, McRuer, Medvec & Galinsky (2019), OBHDP 152, 64-83, six experiments. MESOs (multiple equivalent simultaneous offers) vs a single package: stronger anchors and better outcomes for the offerer (recipients saw them as more sincere), greater joint outcomes, and a more cooperative climate. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.01.007. Abstract only; participant numbers not retrieved. — [Macquarie](https://researchers.mq.edu.au/en/publications/multiple-equivalent-simultaneous-offers-mesos-reduce-the-negotiat/)
- Thompson (1991), JESP 27(2)? (a search result said 40(2), 161-179; volume/pages inconsistent, check) "Information exchange in negotiation". Giving and seeking information both improved accuracy of judgment and produced more integrative agreements, even when only one side did so. Abstract only. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/1991/information-exchange-in-negotiation)
- Thompson & Hastie (1990), Org. Behav. Human Decis. Processes, "Judgment tasks and biases in negotiation" (my memory for the title; the page said "Social perception in negotiation"-type content; check): fixed-sum assumption is widespread; people who missed integrative potential got lower individual and joint profit; many learn through negotiation. Abstract level. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/1990/judgment-tasks-and-biases-in-negotiation/)
- Bazerman & Neale (1983) is the origin of the biases framework (secondary source only). A 2002 JBDM study on initial perceptions found logrolling offers were not judged more attractive, did not dispel the fixed-pie assumption, but still gave the initiator and the pair higher profit. — [CRIS HUJI](https://cris.huji.ac.il/en/publications/initial-perceptions-in-negotiations-evaluation-and-response-to-lo-2/)
- Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017), JPSP 113(3), 430-452. Question-asking, especially follow-up questions, increased liking via perceived responsiveness; people do not predict this. This is about liking in conversation (including speed dating), not negotiation outcomes. DOI 10.1037/pspi0000097. Open author copy at Harvard DASH. Abstract only. — [DASH](https://dash.harvard.edu/entities/publication/73120379-2eb6-6bd4-e053-0100007fdf3b)
- De Dreu, Weingart & Kwon (2000), JPSP 78, 889-905. Meta-analysis of 28 studies: prosocial negotiators were less contentious, solved problems more and got higher joint outcomes, but only when resistance to yielding was high or unknown. No effect size retrieved. — [UvA DARE](https://dare.uva.nl/id/403ebedc-c455-47a0-8a00-803afaed87b3)
- Thompson, Wang & Gunia (2010), Annual Review of Psychology 61, 491-515, "Negotiation": review at five levels (intrapersonal, interpersonal, group, organizational, virtual) on value creation and claiming. Contents not read. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/2010/negotiation/)
- Petrowsky 2025 and Gunia 2013 (section 1): first-offer effects shrink with more issues and act through distributive issues.

### Inferences
- Offering 2-3 equivalent packages that vary price, payment days, contract length and delivery should combine anchoring with logrolling

- Fisher/Ury/Patton and Shell: widely adopted (Harvard PON, Program on Negotiation, associated with the Harvard Negotiation Project) but criticised by scholars for limited empirical testing and for underplaying distributive bargaining [M].

### Inferences
- For a bot-vs-bot, scored setting, popular emotional tactics (mirroring, labels) have little direct value; the numeric principles (anchoring, concession patterns, BATNA, trade-offs across issues) matter more.

### Gaps
- No peer-reviewed or Negotiation Journal review of Voss found; a targeted search of *Negotiation Journal* is needed.

## Which are available via the TUM library or open access?

### Takeaway
TUM runs a catalogue at search.ub.tum.de (VuFind) and offers 300,000+ e-books incl. about 70,000 Springer titles via eAccess; I found no evidence of Oxford/Cambridge e-book packages. I could not verify holdings for any individual title.

### Cited Findings
- TUM University Library licensed Springer Book Archives subject areas, giving about 70,000 Springer eBooks (2015 news item); other page says over 300,000 scientific e-books — [UB TUM news](https://ub.tum.de/en/news?page=105), [UB TUM](https://www.ub.tum.de/en/node/5558). Dated; recheck.
- Access is via TUM ID (eAccess); licence terms forbid systematic downloading — [UB TUM](https://www.ub.tum.de/en/node/5558).
- Oxford University Press mentioned only for e-journals since January 2024; Wiley, Sage, T&F as e-journals — [UB TUM](https://www.ub.tum.de/en/node/5558).
- The TUM catalogue does index at least the Elgar *Research Handbook on Gender and Negotiation* (a record exists at [search.ub.tum.de](https://search.ub.tum.de/vufind/Record/DE-604.BV047089845?lng=en)); this shows the catalogue is searchable but not that it holds the other titles.
- Elgar offers the Olekalns/Adair handbook as eBook for purchase — [Elgar](https://www.e-elgar.com/shop/handbook-of-research-on-negotiation).
- Pearson offers an eTextbook (subscription/rental, DRM-locked platform) for Thompson; Cengage sells eTextbook for Handfield et al. — links above. DRM status presumed [M].

### Inferences
- Springer-published titles (none of the headline books above) would be most likely to be free via TUM. Most listed books are from Pearson, Cengage, McGraw-Hill, Penguin, HBR Press: expect physical library loan (search.ub.tum.de, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek) or purchase. Check via TUM catalogue before buying.
- No open-access full text of the main textbooks found; none should be sought via unauthorised copies.

### Gaps
- Per-title TUM holdings unchecked (catalogue search not executed); Primo use at TUM unconfirmed (TUM appears to use VuFind/OPAC).
- Oxford/Cambridge e-book access at TUM unconfirmed.

## Ranked reading list (summary; ranking is my judgement for an AI buyer agent)

| # | Book | Edition / year | Evidence type | Access |
|---|------|----------------|---------------|--------|
| 1 | Raiffa, Richardson, Metcalfe, *Negotiation Analysis* [M] | Harvard UP, 2002 | Research, formal | Buy/loan; unverified |
| 2 | Thompson, *Mind and Heart of the Negotiator* [V] | 7th, Pearson 2020 | Research-based textbook | Buy / eText (DRM) / loan |
| 3 | Lewicki, Barry, Saunders, *Negotiation* [V] | 8th, McGraw-Hill 2020 | Research-based textbook | Buy/loan |
| 4 | Malhotra and Bazerman, *Negotiation Genius* [partly V] | Bantam 2007 | Research-informed, practitioner-friendly | Buy/loan |
| 5 | Bazerman and Moore, *Judgment in Managerial Decision Making* [M] | Wiley, recent ed. | Research | Buy/loan |
| 6 | Lax and Sebenius, *3-D Negotiation* [V on content] | HBS Press 2006 | Practitioner plus academic | Buy/loan |
| 7 | Raiffa, *Art and Science of Negotiation* [partly V] | Harvard UP 1982 | Research/analytic classic | Buy/loan |
| 8 | Fisher, Ury, Patton, *Getting to Yes* [V] | 3rd, Penguin 2011 | Practitioner framework | Buy/loan |
| 9 | Olekalns and Adair (eds.), *Handbook of Research on Negotiation* [V] | Elgar 2013 | Research handbook | Elgar eBook; library |
| 10 | Gelfand and Brett (eds.), *Handbook of Negotiation and Culture* [V] | SUP 2004 | Research handbook | Buy/loan |
| 11 | Croson and Bolton (eds.), *Oxford Handbook of Economic Conflict Resolution* [V] | OUP | Research (experimental economics) | OUP Academic; library |
| 12 | Shell, *Bargaining for Advantage* [M] | Penguin | Practitioner | Buy/loan |
| 13 | van Weele and Rozemeijer, *Procurement and SCM* [V] | 8th, Cengage 2022 | Textbook | Buy/loan |
| 14 | Handfield et al., *Purchasing and SCM* [V] | 8th, Cengage 2026 | Textbook | Buy/eText/loan |
| 15 | Cousins et al., *Strategic Supply Management* [M] | FT Prentice Hall 2008 | Textbook/theory | Buy/loan |
| 16 | Chopra, *Supply Chain Management* [V] | 7th, Pearson 2018 | Textbook (limited negotiation) | Buy/loan |
| 17 | Voss and Raz, *Never Split the Difference* [M] | Harper Business 2016 | Practitioner opinion | Buy/loan |
| 18 | Kraljic (1983) HBR article, Gelderman and van Weele papers [M] | Journal articles | Research (segmentation) | HBR purchase; library |

Many [M] entries need a follow-up verification pass (editions, publishers, Scholar counts).

1	# Core experimental findings on bargaining behaviour (for an e-mail buyer agent with multi-issue term sheets)
2	
3	Method note: web research only (about 15 search/fetch calls), no Tacto API. Everything below comes from search-result abstracts and publisher/repository pages. I read NO full texts. "Access" is my guess unless stated. Items marked [UNVERIFIED] came from my memory or a single secondary page and need a DOI check. Nearly all studies are lab or online experiments with students or panel participants, not field data.
4	
5	## 1. First offers and anchoring
6	
7	### Takeaway
8	The first-offer effect is large and robust in simple, single-issue, price-type bargaining, and it holds across power, culture and multi-issue settings. Its costs are impasse risk and lower benefit as complexity rises. Extreme offers anchor but can offend and cause walk-aways, especially from low-power recipients. Effect sizes come from one 2025 meta-analysis and are not final-paper verified.
9	
10	### Cited Findings
11	- Meta-analysis of 90 studies (Petrowsky, Loschelder et al., OBHDP 2025, preregistered, robust variance estimation) plus experiments (Studies 2a-2b, N = 2,121). Making the first offer gives an advantage and ambitious first offers give economic gains, but ambitious offers raise impasse odds. Effects shrink as the number and type of issues increase, and the mechanisms change. Conference abstract values: first-mover g = 0.49, first-offer magnitude g = 1.30, offer-outcome r = 0.53 (pre-publication figures, check against the final paper). Heterogeneity is high. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2025.104448. Access: the journal is paywalled, but a Leuphana PubData parallel publication (DOI 10.48548/pubdata-3207) appears open access. Abstract level only. — [Leuphana PubData](https://pubdata.leuphana.de/entities/publication/29dc7e5d-01eb-420a-b73d-66e0be7cd440); [FIS Leuphana summary](https://fis.leuphana.de/en/publications/the-power-and-peril-of-first-offers-in-negotiations-a-conceptual-/)
12	- Galinsky & Mussweiler (2001), JPSP 81(4), 657-669. Three lab experiments: first offers anchor outcomes, and the effect is reduced when the counterpart takes perspective or focuses on their own target/BATNA information. DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.81.4.657 [UNVERIFIED, from memory]. APA/library access (TUM). Abstract only. — [Kellogg record](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/2001/first-offers-as-anchors-the-role-of-perspective-taking)
13	- Orr & Guthrie (2006), Ohio State J. on Dispute Resolution 21, 597; meta-analysis of simulated negotiations. Anchoring has a significant effect on deals, tested against experience and information environment. A secondary blog gives r about 0.50 (0.37 adjusted for experience); verify before use. Open access on bepress. Abstract only. — [bepress](https://works.bepress.com/chris-guthrie/18); [Vanderbilt IR](https://ir.vanderbilt.edu/handle/1803/7415); secondary: [Miles Mediation](https://milesmediation.com/blog/make-the-first-move-and-drop-the-anchor-miles-mediation/)
14	- Gunia, Swaab, Sivanathan & Galinsky (2013), PSPB 39, 1547-1558, "Remarkable robustness of the first-offer effect: across culture, power, and issues". The effect held across cultures and in multi-issue negotiations, and low-power negotiators gained from moving first. The first offer works through the distributive issues, not the integrative or compatible ones. DOI not retrieved. Abstract only. Lab. — [LBS record](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/t/the-remarkable-robustness-of-the-first-offer-effect-across-culture-power-and-issues)
15	- Extreme offers: Schweinsberg, Ku, Wang & Pillutla (2012), JESP 48(1), 226-231, "Starting high and ending with nothing". Two experiments. Extreme first offers still anchor counteroffers and outcomes, but they offend recipients and risk impasse. Low-power and high-power recipients were equally offended, but low-power ones walked away. Abstract only. (A search note said the Kellogg subtitle differs; I did not check author order or the DOI.) — [LBS](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/s/starting-high-and-ending-with-nothing-the-role-of-anchors-and-power-in-negotiations); [ISB](https://eprints.exchange.isb.edu/id/eprint/1559/)
16	- Precision: Loschelder, Friese & Trötschel (2017), JESP 70, 164-176, three experiments. Precise anchors (e.g. 4,970 vs 5,000) anchor recipients more strongly, via an attribution of competence. Senders who use precise numbers choose less extreme (less ambitious) offers. Abstract level only; no effect sizes retrieved. — [Saarland repository](https://publikationen.sulb.uni-saarland.de/handle/20.500.11880/27829); [PON summary](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/dealmaking-daily/negotiation-research-can-use-effective-first-offer-strive-precision-nb/?amp)
17	- Mussweiler & Strack (1999), JESP 35, 136-164, is the selective accessibility account of anchoring (anchor-consistent knowledge becomes more accessible). Harris et al. (2019) report failures to replicate a key result of that theory (UCL preprint; not read). I did not find a direct Many Labs anchoring replication via search; my memory says Many Labs 1 replicated classic anchoring, but this is unverified. — [LBS record](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/a/anchoring-accessibility-as-a-cause-of-judgmental-assimilation); [UCL](https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10074759/1/HarrisEtAl_2019_anchoring.pdf)
18	- Brooks & Schweitzer (2011), OBHDP 115, 43-54: incidental anxiety lowered expectations and opening offers and worsened outcomes (four studies; HBS summary says $6.60 vs $7.94 in one study). Relevant only as evidence that low aspirations lower first offers. — [IDEAS](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v115y2011i1p43-54.html); [HBS](https://hbswk.hbs.edu/item/overcoming-nervous-nelly)
19	
20	### Inferences
21	- For a buyer agent, anchor first with an ambitious but defensible opening, and keep it believable; reserve extreme offers for situations where walking away is not costly. This is an inference from Petrowsky, Schweinsberg and the Leonardelli entries below.
22	- With a precise (non-round) opening figure, the recipient may be anchored more strongly, but the agent should not shrink its ambition because of it. This is my inference from Loschelder et al.
23	- In a multi-issue term sheet the anchor effect is concentrated in the price (distributive) issue (Gunia 2013) and weakens as issues multiply (Petrowsky 2025).
24	
25	### Gaps
26	- Final effect sizes, moderator tables and the exact impasse increase from Petrowsky 2025 were not read.
27	- No direct evidence on anchoring in e-mail or LLM-vs-LLM negotiation was found.
28	- Replication status of the negotiation-specific effects: no failed replication of the first-offer effect found; the replication of the cognitive mechanism is contested (Harris 2019).
29	
30	## 2. Concession patterns
31	
32	### Takeaway
33	Hard bargaining wins more money but costs relationship and, in some conditions, impasses. Reciprocating concessions is the best soft strategy. Shrinking concession steps signal a nearing limit and make recipients less ambitious; the evidence is a single 2021 lab paper plus older work.
34	
35	### Cited Findings
36	- Hüffmeier, Freund, Zerres, Backhaus & Hertel (2014), J. Management 40(3), 866-892. Meta-analysis of 34 studies of distributive negotiation (135 economic and 30 socioemotional effect sizes). Hardline strategies gave higher economic outcomes and softline gave higher socioemotional outcomes. Hardliners gained most with visual contact, knowledge of the bargaining zone and a maximize-own-outcome instruction. Softliners did best when they accurately reciprocated concessions, and softline did not win even when impasse risk and cost were high (contrary to prediction). DOI 10.1177/0149206311423788. Likely paywalled (TUM). Abstract only; no d/r values retrieved. — [UvA DARE](https://dare.uva.nl/id/801197e8-e374-4128-aeb3-c66c06cb8812)
37	- Tey, Schaerer, Madan & Swaab (2021), OBHDP 165, 153-166. Seven studies, N = 2,311. Decreasing concession sequences (e.g. 1,500, 1,210, 1,180, 1,170) lead recipients to make less ambitious counteroffers and reach worse deals, mediated by an inflated estimate of the counterpart's reservation price. The effect is strongest for moderate decline rates and for declines over more rounds; setting a target in advance partly protects recipients. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2021.05.003. Abstract only. Lab/online. — [INSEAD](https://www.insead.edu/faculty-research/publications/journal-articles/impact-concession-patterns-negotiations-when-and-why)
38	- Lawler & MacMurray (1980), a programmed-opponent study cited in a search snippet: the best response depended on the opponent's opening stance, and prior deadlock reduced concessions. Single secondary snippet, not verified. — [Leuphana snippet](https://fis.leuphana.de/en/publications/concession-patterns-in-dyadic-negotiations-empirically-contrastin/)
39	- A separate study (found via the same search, authors not retrieved) reports that distributive concession making raises impasse rates, driven by loss of conceded value and not by reciprocity-norm violation. — [TU Dortmund](https://eldorado.tu-dortmund.de/items/f909800c-1d5e-4cb0-9fa9-9745ab154670/full)
40	
41	### Inferences
42	- A seller-facing buyer agent should avoid showing a clear shrinking-step pattern if it wants to hide its limit, and should expect a seller using one to be signalling a limit (but it may be a bluff).
43	- Reciprocate counterpart concessions in kind; start tough and concede on a pattern that does not leak the limit.
44	
45	### Gaps
46	- No meta-analysis on concession timing found; no evidence tied specifically to e-mail asynchronous bargaining.
47	- Effect sizes of Hüffmeier 2014 not retrieved.
48	
49	## 3. BATNA, reservation prices and power
50	
51	### Takeaway
52	Better alternatives raise outcomes and the propensity to move first, but the first-offer anchor can outweigh BATNA effects and, per one study, having no BATNA can beat a weak one. Evidence on disclosing information is weak in my findings.
53	
54	### Cited Findings
55	- Kim & Fragale (2005), J. Applied Psychology 90(2), 373-381. BATNA advantage mattered more when the bargaining zone was small, contribution advantage when it was large. DOI 10.1037/0021-9010.90.2.373 (as found by search; not opened). Abstract level. — [summary page](https://academicnewsletter.sufe.edu.cn/info/372348)
56	- Magee, Galinsky & Gruenfeld (2007), PSPB 33(2), 200-212. Five experiments. Higher power increased propensity to negotiate and to move first; negotiators with strong BATNAs were over three times as likely to intend to open (as reported by the abstract summary); making the first offer gave a bargaining edge. Abstract only. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/2007/power-propensity-to-negotiate-and-moving-first-in-competitive/?p=1)
57	- Pinkley, Neale & Bennett (1994), OBHDP 57(1), 97-116, "The impact of alternatives to settlement in dyadic negotiation". Content not retrieved; only the citation. A 1995 Pinkley OBHDP paper on BATNA knowledge was not confirmed. — [IDEAS](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v57y1994i1p97-116.html)
58	- Schaerer, Swaab & Galinsky, Psychological Science (about 2015; year and title unconfirmed): negotiators with no BATNA did better than those with weak BATNAs, because they made higher first offers (anchors weigh more than power). Seen only in a search note; [UNVERIFIED]. — [APS](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/minds-business/negotiating-with-nothing-holds-surprise-benefits.html)
59	- Schweinsberg et al. 2012 (section 1): power moderates whether extreme anchors lead to walk-aways.
60	- Gunia, Brett, Nandkeolyar & Kamdar (2011), J. Applied Psychology 96(4), 774-789, three studies: lower interpersonal trust in Indian negotiators went with less information-sharing and lower joint gains than for US negotiators. Relevant to information exchange, not BATNA. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/2011/paying-a-price-culture-trust-and-negotiation-consequences/?p=1)
61	- Kong, Dirks & Ferrin (2014), Acad. Management J. 57(5), 1235-1255. Meta-analysis of 38 independent studies on trust within negotiations, with three contingencies. Effect sizes not retrieved. — [MetaTOC](https://metatoc.com/papers/23303-interpersonal-trust-within-negotiations-meta-analytic-evidence-critical-contingencies-and-directions-for-future-research)
62	
63	### Inferences
64	- A buyer agent should have its BATNA/reservation value internally and may move first when its BATNA is good, but should not reveal the reservation price (no direct evidence retrieved on disclosure; this is a design judgment). Evidence is largely lab.
65	
66	### Gaps
67	- Evidence on disclosing versus hiding BATNA/reservation price (Pinkley 1995, Morris/Larrick/Su, Gunia et al. alternatives) was not retrieved. Treat as open.
68	- Replication status of the weak-BATNA result is unknown.
69	
70	## 4. Multi-issue offers, MESOs, logrolling, questions, information
71	
72	### Takeaway
73	MESOs, information exchange and question-asking raise joint gains and rapport in lab studies; the fixed-pie bias is the main obstacle. A buyer agent sending packages with several equivalent options should gain both anchoring and integrative benefits. The evidence is lab-based.
74	
75	### Cited Findings
76	- Leonardelli, Gu, McRuer, Medvec & Galinsky (2019), OBHDP 152, 64-83, six experiments. MESOs (multiple equivalent simultaneous offers) vs a single package: stronger anchors and better outcomes for the offerer (recipients saw them as more sincere), greater joint outcomes, and a more cooperative climate. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.01.007. Abstract only; participant numbers not retrieved. — [Macquarie](https://researchers.mq.edu.au/en/publications/multiple-equivalent-simultaneous-offers-mesos-reduce-the-negotiat/)
77	- Thompson (1991), JESP 27(2)? (a search result said 40(2), 161-179; volume/pages inconsistent, check) "Information exchange in negotiation". Giving and seeking information both improved accuracy of judgment and produced more integrative agreements, even when only one side did so. Abstract only. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/1991/information-exchange-in-negotiation)
78	- Thompson & Hastie (1990), Org. Behav. Human Decis. Processes, "Judgment tasks and biases in negotiation" (my memory for the title; the page said "Social perception in negotiation"-type content; check): fixed-sum assumption is widespread; people who missed integrative potential got lower individual and joint profit; many learn through negotiation. Abstract level. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/1990/judgment-tasks-and-biases-in-negotiation/)
79	- Bazerman & Neale (1983) is the origin of the biases framework (secondary source only). A 2002 JBDM study on initial perceptions found logrolling offers were not judged more attractive, did not dispel the fixed-pie assumption, but still gave the initiator and the pair higher profit. — [CRIS HUJI](https://cris.huji.ac.il/en/publications/initial-perceptions-in-negotiations-evaluation-and-response-to-lo-2/)
80	- Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017), JPSP 113(3), 430-452. Question-asking, especially follow-up questions, increased liking via perceived responsiveness; people do not predict this. This is about liking in conversation (including speed dating), not negotiation outcomes. DOI 10.1037/pspi0000097. Open author copy at Harvard DASH. Abstract only. — [DASH](https://dash.harvard.edu/entities/publication/73120379-2eb6-6bd4-e053-0100007fdf3b)
81	- De Dreu, Weingart & Kwon (2000), JPSP 78, 889-905. Meta-analysis of 28 studies: prosocial negotiators were less contentious, solved problems more and got higher joint outcomes, but only when resistance to yielding was high or unknown. No effect size retrieved. — [UvA DARE](https://dare.uva.nl/id/403ebedc-c455-47a0-8a00-803afaed87b3)
82	- Thompson, Wang & Gunia (2010), Annual Review of Psychology 61, 491-515, "Negotiation": review at five levels (intrapersonal, interpersonal, group, organizational, virtual) on value creation and claiming. Contents not read. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/2010/negotiation/)
83	- Petrowsky 2025 and Gunia 2013 (section 1): first-offer effects shrink with more issues and act through distributive issues.
84	
85	### Inferences
86	- Offering 2-3 equivalent packages that vary price, payment days, contract length and delivery should combine anchoring with logrolling; ask about counterpart priorities (questions plus sharing own preferences) before settling.
87	- Question-asking effects on liking may carry to rapport in e-mail, but there is no direct negotiation-outcome evidence in what I retrieved.
88	
89	### Gaps
90	- A Huang et al.-style test of question-asking in negotiation outcomes (e.g. Minson/Brooks work) was not retrieved.
91	- Fixed-pie quantitative effect sizes, Loewenstein/Thompson/Bazerman details, and replication status of MESO and logrolling studies are unknown.
92	- Whether MESOs work in written/e-mail or agent settings: not found.
93	
94	## Source access summary
95	Open or likely open: Orr & Guthrie (bepress), Petrowsky 2025 via Leuphana parallel publication, Huang 2017 (DASH). Likely TUM/library: Galinsky & Mussweiler, Leonardelli, Hüffmeier, Kong, De Dreu et al., Tey et al., Thompson/Wang/Gunia, Kim & Fragale, Magee et al., Gunia et al.
96

- Precision: Loschelder, Friese & Trötschel (2017), JESP 70, 164-176, three experiments. Precise anchors (e.g. 4,970 vs 5,000) anchor recipients more strongly, via an attribution of competence. Senders who use precise numbers choose less extreme (less ambitious) offers. Abstract level only; no effect sizes retrieved. — [Saarland repository](https://publikationen.sulb.uni-saarland.de/handle/20.500.11880/27829); [PON summary](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/dealmaking-daily/negotiation-research-can-use-effective-first-offer-strive-precision-nb/?amp)
- Mussweiler & Strack (1999), JESP 35, 136-164, is the selective accessibility account of anchoring (anchor-consistent knowledge becomes more accessible). Harris et al. (2019) report failures to replicate a key result of that theory (UCL preprint; not read). I did not find a direct Many Labs anchoring replication via search; my memory says Many Labs 1 replicated classic anchoring, but this is unverified. — [LBS record](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/a/anchoring-accessibility-as-a-cause-of-judgmental-assimilation); [UCL](https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10074759/1/HarrisEtAl_2019_anchoring.pdf)
- Brooks & Schweitzer (2011), OBHDP 115, 43-54: incidental anxiety lowered expectations and opening offers and worsened outcomes (four studies; HBS summary says $6.60 vs $7.94 in one study). Relevant only as evidence that low aspirations lower first offers. — [IDEAS](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v115y2011i1p43-54.html); [HBS](https://hbswk.hbs.edu/item/overcoming-nervous-nelly)

### Inferences
- For a buyer agent, anchor first with an ambitious but defensible opening, and keep it believable; reserve extreme offers for situations where walking away is not costly. This is an inference from Petrowsky, Schweinsberg and the Leonardelli entries below.
- With a precise (non-round) opening figure, the recipient may be anchored more strongly, but the agent should not shrink its ambition because of it. This is my inference from Loschelder et al.
- In a multi-issue term sheet the anchor effect is concentrated in the price (distributive) issue (Gunia 2013) and weakens as issues multiply (Petrowsky 2025).

### Gaps
- Final effect sizes, moderator tables and the exact impasse increase from Petrowsky 2025 were not read.
- No direct evidence on anchoring in e-mail or LLM-vs-LLM negotiation was found.
- Replication status of the negotiation-specific effects: no failed replication of the first-offer effect found; the replication of the cognitive mechanism is contested (Harris 2019).

## 2. Concession patterns

### Takeaway
Hard bargaining wins more money but costs relationship and, in some conditions, impasses. Reciprocating concessions is the best soft strategy. Shrinking concession steps signal a nearing limit and make recipients less ambitious; the evidence is a single 2021 lab paper plus older work.

### Cited Findings
- Hüffmeier, Freund, Zerres, Backhaus & Hertel (2014), J. Management 40(3), 866-892. Meta-analysis of 34 studies of distributive negotiation (135 economic and 30 socioemotional effect sizes). Hardline strategies gave higher economic outcomes and softline gave higher socioemotional outcomes. Hardliners gained most with visual contact, knowledge of the bargaining zone and a maximize-own-outcome instruction. Softliners did best when they accurately reciprocated concessions, and softline did not win even when impasse risk and cost were high (contrary to prediction). DOI 10.1177/0149206311423788. Likely paywalled (TUM). Abstract only; no d/r values retrieved. — [UvA DARE](https://dare.uva.nl/id/801197e8-e374-4128-aeb3-c66c06cb8812)
- Tey, Schaerer, Madan & Swaab (2021), OBHDP 165, 153-166. Seven studies, N = 2,311. Decreasing concession sequences (e.g. 1,500, 1,210, 1,180, 1,170) lead recipients to make less ambitious counteroffers and reach worse deals, mediated by an inflated estimate of the counterpart's reservation price. The effect is strongest for moderate decline rates and for declines over more rounds; setting a target in advance partly protects recipients. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2021.05.003. Abstract only. Lab/online. — [INSEAD](https://www.insead.edu/faculty-research/publications/journal-articles/impact-concession-patterns-negotiations-when-and-why)
- Lawler & MacMurray (1980), a programmed-opponent study cited in a search snippet: the best response depended on the opponent's opening stance, and prior deadlock reduced concessions. Single secondary snippet, not verified. — [Leuphana snippet](https://fis.leuphana.de/en/publications/concession-patterns-in-dyadic-negotiations-empirically-contrastin/)
- A separate study (found via the same search, authors not retrieved) reports that distributive concession making raises impasse rates, driven by loss of conceded value and not by reciprocity-norm violation. — [TU Dortmund](https://eldorado.tu-dortmund.de/items/f909800c-1d5e-4cb0-9fa9-9745ab154670/full)

### Inferences
- A seller-facing buyer agent should avoid showing a clear shrinking-step pattern if it wants to hide its limit, and should expect a seller using one to be signalling a limit (but it may be a bluff).
- Reciprocate counterpart concessions in kind; start tough and concede on a pattern that does not leak the limit.

### Gaps
- No meta-analysis on concession timing found; no evidence tied specifically to e-mail asynchronous bargaining.
- Effect sizes of Hüffmeier 2014 not retrieved.

## 3. BATNA, reservation prices and power

### Takeaway
Better alternatives raise outcomes and the propensity to move first, but the first-offer anchor can outweigh BATNA effects and, per one study, having no BATNA can beat a weak one. Evidence on disclosing information is weak in my findings.

### Cited Findings
- Kim & Fragale (2005), J. Applied Psychology 90(2), 373-381. BATNA advantage mattered more when the bargaining zone was small, contribution advantage when it was large. DOI 10.1037/0021-9010.90.2.373 (as found by search; not opened). Abstract level. — [summary page](https://academicnewsletter.sufe.edu.cn/info/372348)
- Magee, Galinsky & Gruenfeld (2007), PSPB 33(2), 200-212. Five experiments. Higher power increased propensity to negotiate and to move first; negotiators with strong BATNAs were over three times as likely to intend to open (as reported by the abstract summary); making the first offer gave a bargaining edge. Abstract only. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/2007/power-propensity-to-negotiate-and-moving-first-in-competitive/?p=1)
- Pinkley, Neale & Bennett (1994), OBHDP 57(1), 97-116, "The impact of alternatives to settlement in dyadic negotiation". Content not retrieved; only the citation. A 1995 Pinkley OBHDP paper on BATNA knowledge was not confirmed. — [IDEAS](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v57y1994i1p97-116.html)
- Schaerer, Swaab & Galinsky, Psychological Science (about 2015; year and title unconfirmed): negotiators with no BATNA did better than those with weak BATNAs, because they made higher first offers (anchors weigh more than power). Seen only in a search note; [UNVERIFIED]. — [APS](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/minds-business/negotiating-with-nothing-holds-surprise-benefits.html)
- Schweinsberg et al. 2012 (section 1): power moderates whether extreme anchors lead to walk-aways.
- Gunia, Brett, Nandkeolyar & Kamdar (2011), J. Applied Psychology 96(4), 774-789, three studies: lower interpersonal trust in Indian negotiators went with less information-sharing and lower joint gains than for US negotiators. Relevant to information exchange, not BATNA. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/2011/paying-a-price-culture-trust-and-negotiation-consequences/?p=1)
- Kong, Dirks & Ferrin (2014), Acad. Management J. 57(5), 1235-1255. Meta-analysis of 38 independent studies on trust within negotiations, with three contingencies. Effect sizes not retrieved. — [MetaTOC](https://metatoc.com/papers/23303-interpersonal-trust-within-negotiations-meta-analytic-evidence-critical-contingencies-and-directions-for-future-research)

### Inferences
- A buyer agent should have its BATNA/reservation value internally and may move first when its BATNA is good, but should not reveal the reservation price (no direct evidence retrieved on disclosure; this is a design judgment). Evidence is largely lab.

### Gaps
- Evidence on disclosing versus hiding BATNA/reservation price (Pinkley 1995, Morris/Larrick/Su, Gunia et al. alternatives) was not retrieved. Treat as open.
- Replication status of the weak-BATNA result is unknown.

## 4. Multi-issue offers, MESOs, logrolling, questions, information

### Takeaway
MESOs, information exchange and question-asking raise joint gains and rapport in lab studies; the fixed-pie bias is the main obstacle. A buyer agent sending packages with several equivalent options should gain both anchoring and integrative benefits. The evidence is lab-based.

### Cited Findings
- Leonardelli, Gu, McRuer, Medvec & Galinsky (2019), OBHDP 152, 64-83, six experiments. MESOs (multiple equivalent simultaneous offers) vs a single package: stronger anchors and better outcomes for the offerer (recipients saw them as more sincere), greater joint outcomes, and a more cooperative climate. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.01.007. Abstract only; participant numbers not retrieved. — [Macquarie](https://researchers.mq.edu.au/en/publications/multiple-equivalent-simultaneous-offers-mesos-reduce-the-negotiat/)
- Thompson (1991), JESP 27(2)? (a search result said 40(2), 161-179; volume/pages inconsistent, check) "Information exchange in negotiation". Giving and seeking information both improved accuracy of judgment and produced more integrative agreements, even when only one side did so. Abstract only. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/1991/information-exchange-in-negotiation)
- Thompson & Hastie (1990), Org. Behav. Human Decis. Processes, "Judgment tasks and biases in negotiation" (my memory for the title; the page said "Social perception in negotiation"-type content; check): fixed-sum assumption is widespread; people who missed integrative potential got lower individual and joint profit; many learn through negotiation. Abstract level. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/1990/judgment-tasks-and-biases-in-negotiation/)
- Bazerman & Neale (1983) is the origin of the biases framework (secondary source only). A 2002 JBDM study on initial perceptions found logrolling offers were not judged more attractive, did not dispel the fixed-pie assumption, but still gave the initiator and the pair higher profit. — [CRIS HUJI](https://cris.huji.ac.il/en/publications/initial-perceptions-in-negotiations-evaluation-and-response-to-lo-2/)
- Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017), JPSP 113(3), 430-452. Question-asking, especially follow-up questions, increased liking via perceived responsiveness; people do not predict this. This is about liking in conversation (including speed dating), not negotiation outcomes. DOI 10.1037/pspi0000097. Open author copy at Harvard DASH. Abstract only. — [DASH](https://dash.harvard.edu/entities/publication/73120379-2eb6-6bd4-e053-0100007fdf3b)
- De Dreu, Weingart & Kwon (2000), JPSP 78, 889-905. Meta-analysis of 28 studies: prosocial negotiators were less contentious, solved problems more and got higher joint outcomes, but only when resistance to yielding was high or unknown. No effect size retrieved. — [UvA DARE](https://dare.uva.nl/id/403ebedc-c455-47a0-8a00-803afaed87b3)
- Thompson, Wang & Gunia (2010), Annual Review of Psychology 61, 491-515, "Negotiation": review at five levels (intrapersonal, interpersonal, group, organizational, virtual) on value creation and claiming. Contents not read. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/2010/negotiation/)
- Petrowsky 2025 and Gunia 2013 (section 1): first-offer effects shrink with more issues and act through distributive issues.

### Inferences
- Offering 2-3 equivalent packages that vary price, payment days, contract length and delivery should combine anchoring with logrolling; ask about counterpart priorities (questions plus sharing own preferences) before settling.
- Question-asking effects on liking may carry to rapport in e-mail, but there is no direct negotiation-outcome evidence in what I retrieved.

### Gaps
- A Huang et al.-style test of question-asking in negotiation outcomes (e.g. Minson/Brooks work) was not retrieved.
- Fixed-pie quantitative effect sizes, Loewenstein/Thompson/Bazerman details, and replication status of MESO and logrolling studies are unknown.
- Whether MESOs work in written/e-mail or agent settings: not found.

## Source access summary
Open or likely open: Orr & Guthrie (bepress), Petrowsky 2025 via Leuphana parallel publication, Huang 2017 (DASH). Likely TUM/library: Galinsky & Mussweiler, Leonardelli, Hüffmeier, Kong, De Dreu et al., Tey et al., Thompson/Wang/Gunia, Kim & Fragale, Magee et al., Gunia et al.

content.content:
1	# Replication status and robustness of classic negotiation/judgment findings
2	
3	Method note: web research only, no Tacto API. Access level for every source below is "snippet/abstract/search summary only" unless stated; NO full text was read. Many figures come from search-engine summaries of pages and are marked "(secondary)". The report writer should treat all numbers as needing verification before being put in code comments. Items marked [prior knowledge] were NOT verified this session.
4	
5	## 1. Anchoring and first-offer advantage
6	
7	### Takeaway
8	Anchoring is among the most robust judgment effects (replicated at scale), and a preregistered 2023 meta-analysis finds a first-mover advantage in negotiation (g about 0.49) and a strong offer-outcome relation. But effects are highly heterogeneous, and "go first" has a subjective-value/impasse cost.
9	
10	### Cited Findings
11	- Many Labs 1 (Klein et al. 2014, Social Psychology, DOI 10.1027/1864-9335/a000178; paywalled at Hogrefe, fetch blocked; library/TUM access likely; abstract-level only via secondary sources): anchoring replicated, with effects reported as larger than the original Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995) in raw terms, though a commentator notes the original effect-size metric was not comparable (test-retest correlation vs. between-subjects) — [Gelman blog on Many Labs](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2014/02/27/can-learn-many-labs-replication-project/), [Scientific American report](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/dozens-of-labs-respond-to-bolster-reliability-of-psychology-research). Secondary only; no d values retrieved.
12	- Many Labs 2 (Klein et al. 2018, AMPPS, DOI 10.1177/2515245918810225, open access; not read): 28 findings, 125 samples, 15,305 participants, 36 countries; median d 0.60 originals vs 0.15 replications across all findings (not anchoring-specific) — [search summary of ML2 records](https://research.monash.edu/en/publications/many-labs-2-investigating-variation-in-replicability-across-sampl/). I could NOT confirm the anchoring row of ML2 in this session.
13	- Orr and Guthrie (2006), "Anchoring, Information, Expertise, and Negotiation: New Insights from Meta-Analysis", Ohio State J. on Dispute Resolution 21:597, 2006 (open via Vanderbilt repository, abstract only): meta-analysis of simulated negotiations; anchors significantly affect outcomes; only partial support for moderation by information environment and negotiator experience — [Vanderbilt IR](https://ir.vanderbilt.edu/handle/1803/7415), [Guthrie page](https://works.bepress.com/chris-guthrie/18). A secondary source quotes r = .497 (.37 adjusted for experience); unverified.
14	- Petrowsky et al. (IACM 2023 conference paper, preregistered meta-analysis; no journal version found; abstract only): first-mover advantage g = 0.49; first-offer magnitude effect g = 1.30; offer-outcome correlation r = .53 (g = 1.51); effects highly heterogeneous, moderated by publication, sample, negotiation and offer characteristics. Harvard PON summary says about 90 studies — [Leuphana abstract](https://fis.leuphana.de/en/activities/a-threefold-meta-analysis-of-economic-first-offer-effects-in-nego/), [PON Daily](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/negotiation-skills-daily/when-to-make-the-first-offer-in-negotiations). Same program reports first-offer analysis of over 25 million eBay negotiations (details unread) — [Leuphana interview](https://www.leuphana.de/en/graduate-school/events/news/single-view/2024/09/13/interview-dr-hannes-m-petrowsky.html). One search summary says a Petrowsky/Loschelder meta-analysis finds ambitious first offers yield fewer deals and lower recipient subjective value; the exact paper/DOI was not confirmed.
15	- Hüffmeier et al. 2014 (J. Management 40(3):866-892; 34 studies): hardline bargaining gives higher economic outcomes, softline higher socioemotional outcomes; hardliners do best with visual contact, male opponent, maximize instructions, known bargaining zone; softliners do best when reciprocating concessions accurately — [DARE UvA record](https://dare.uva.nl/id/801197e8-e374-4128-aeb3-c66c06cb8812). Abstract only.
16	
17	### Inferences
18	- Label "anchor / extreme-but-credible first offer when you have info advantage": strong for the anchoring mechanism, moderate for first-mover advantage (meta-analytic, heterogeneous, student-heavy), weak for "always go first": impasse risk and relationship cost are documented.
19	- Dynamic nuance: a deal-always-wanted agent should cap ambition to avoid impasse; the meta-analytic mean hides this.
20	
21	### Gaps
22	- Klein 2014 and 2018 anchoring effect sizes not retrieved (paywall/blocked). Furnham and Boo 2011 review not searched. Go-second (counter-anchoring) evidence not found. Petrowsky journal version/DOI and k not found.
23	
24	## 2. Power and power priming; BATNA
25	
26	### Takeaway
27	Postural/priming power effects on behavior and hormones failed to replicate; feeling-powerful self-report survives. Negotiation-specific power-pose tests showed no outcome advantage. Alternatives/BATNA as structural power is not tested by those failures, but I found no meta-analysis here.
28	
29	### Cited Findings
30	- Power-pose behavioral effects did not replicate across a 2017 special issue; Carney stopped endorsing hormonal effects; small effect on felt power remains — [Power pose overview (Wikipedia)](https://Www.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_pose), [Futurity summary](https://www.futurity.org/power-poses-1539282-2/). Low-quality secondary sources.
31	- Cesario and Johnson's negotiation experiment: power-posers did no better than partners — same summaries above (secondary).
32	- A BI Norwegian Business School study manipulating power via BATNA asymmetry and priming found no significant results — [BI Open record](https://biopen.bi.no/bi-xmlui/handle/11250/2484417?show=full). Abstract only; small study.
33	
34	### Inferences
35	- "Prime yourself powerful / power pose": weak. "Improve your BATNA / know the counterpart's": plausible and theoretically central, but I did not find replication-grade evidence either way; label moderate (theory plus non-replicated-priming caveat), pending sources such as Schaerer et al. 2018 [prior knowledge].
36	
37	### Gaps
38	- Galinsky et al. original power papers and Schaerer et al. (2018) power-in-negotiation review not retrieved; no direct meta-analysis of BATNA effect.
39	
40	## 3. Emotion, gender, culture
41	
42	### Takeaway
43	Anger-concession effect replicated directly (Pollmann 2017) but a Many Labs 5 replication of a related van Dijk 2008 design found only a weak effect (one ninth of original), so label moderate/fragile. Gender gap is small and context-dependent (Mazei 2015). Culture: single studies, no robust meta-analysis found.
44	
45	### Cited Findings
46	- Pollmann et al. 2017 (Dutch-language direct replication of Van Kleef et al. 2004; Tilburg): anger drew larger concessions than happiness, medium effect — [AUP Online record](https://aup-online.com/content/journals/10.5117/2017.045.002.008), [Tilburg record](https://research.tilburguniversity.edu/en/publications/boosheid-en-blijdschap-in-onderhandelingen-een-replicatie-van-van/). Abstract level; summary says other conceptual replications show different patterns.
47	- Many Labs 5 / Skorb et al. 2020, AMPPS (DOI 10.1177/2515245920927643): replication of van Dijk et al. 2008; effect about one ninth of original, significant only under the revised protocol; FLoRA classes as mixed — [AMPPS page](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/ampps/2515245920927643/), [FLoRA atlas](https://forrt.org/flora-replication-atlas/doi/10.1037/0022-3514.94.4.600/). Abstract only. Original used low-consequence-of-rejection condition.
48	- Sinaceur et al. 2011: threats may beat anger — [Bath portal](https://researchportal.bath.ac.uk/en/publications/hot-or-cold-is-communicating-anger-or-threats-more-effective-in-n/). Abstract only.
49	- Mazei et al. 2015, Psychological Bulletin 141(1):85-104, DOI 10.1037/a0038184: 123 effect sizes, N = 10,888; men achieve modestly better economic outcomes on average (d about 0.20, secondary); gap shrinks with prior experience, bargaining-range info, or negotiating for others, and reverses in some conditions — [Münster CRIS](https://cris-portal.uni-muenster.de/portal/en/publication/23890464), [Newswise](https://www.newswise.com/articles/women-outperform-men-in-some-financial-negotiations-research-finds). Abstract only.
50	- Aslani et al. 2016, J. Organizational Behavior 37(8):1178-1201 (NOT a meta-analysis; no Gelfand author): honor and face culture negotiators used more competitive strategies than dignity-culture negotiators; three intracultural samples (USA, China, Qatar) — [Vlerick repository](https://repository.vlerick.com/handle/20.500.12127/7616).
51	
52	### Inferences
53	- Anger-as-tactic: moderate-to-weak; sign depends on context (consequences of rejection, power). Gender: small, moderated; do not encode gender-based rules. Culture: weak for rule-making (few samples, no meta-analytic robustness found).
54	
55	### Gaps
56	- Van Kleef 2004 original and any anger meta-analysis not found. Gelfand culture-and-negotiation meta-analysis (Gunia/Brett or Gelfand work) not found.
57	
58	## 4. Fixed-pie bias, logrolling, and training
59	
60	### Takeaway
61	Fixed-pie perceptions are well documented but variable in size; training has positive effects with limited systematic evidence (Movius 2008). Note: Hüffmeier 2014 is NOT a training meta-analysis.
62	
63	### Cited Findings
64	- Fixed-pie bias origin and persistence (Bazerman; Thompson and Hastie 1990); Pinkley, Griffith and Northcraft 1995 found fixed-pie expectations cause suboptimal agreements; a role-play study found only a minority showed the bias; Japanese study suggests task-structure artifact; Kern, Brett, Weingart and Eck 2020 (OBHDP 157:143-158) ran an internal meta-analysis of context effects on fixed-pie perceptions — [Cambridge chapter](https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/292F0EF15217DE3D95988A01944728B4/core-reader), [IDEAS record for Kern et al. 2020](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v157y2020icp143-158.html), [Springer study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/B:GRUP.0000031089.91654.26). Search-summary level; details not verified.
65	- Movius 2008, Negotiation Journal 24(4):509-531, DOI 10.1111/j.1571-9979.2008.00201.x: reviews evidence on negotiation training across four outcome levels; evidence sparse but suggests positive effects — [CBI page](https://www.cbi.org/article/2008/effectiveness-of-negotiation-training/). Abstract only; full text on Wiley (TUM likely).
66	- Zerres, Hüffmeier et al. 2013, J. Applied Psychology: bilateral training beats no training, effect stable over time; unilateral training only effective for sellers — [UvA DARE](https://dare.uva.nl/id/cf4737e6-d64f-4856-922b-ebd06ba8e763). Abstract only.
67	- Sondern, Nohe et al. 2019: "Effectiveness of negotiation trainings: a meta-analysis" (conference contribution, findings not retrieved) — [Münster CRIS](https://cris-portal.uni-muenster.de/portal/en/publication/60580628).
68	- Maddux, Mullen and Galinsky 2008 (JESP 44:461-468): strategic mimicry increased individual and joint gains and deal likelihood in two experiments, mediated by trust — [Kellogg page](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/2008/chameleons-bake-bigger-pies-and-take-bigger-pieces-strategic), [SSOAR PDF](https://www.ssoar.info/ssoar/bitstream/document/21568/1/ssoar-jexpsocpsychol-2008-2-maddux_et_al-chameleons_bake_bigger_pies_and.pdf). Abstract-level; this is the nearest peer-reviewed support for "mirroring" (behavioral mimicry, not verbal repetition); small lab study, replication status unknown.
69	
70	### Inferences
71	- "Search for compatible/different-priority issues and logroll": moderate-to-strong in theory and lab, but the exact effect size not verified. Training: moderate.
72	
73	### Gaps
74	- Hüffmeier is not the training meta-analyst; the user-prompted attribution is wrong. Thompson/Loewenstein training papers and strategic-adaptability training not retrieved. No Many-Labs-grade replication of fixed-pie bias found.
75	
76	## 5. Popular advice: Voss tactics, Getting to Yes
77	
78	### Takeaway
79	No peer-reviewed controlled test of Voss's "mirroring (verbal repetition)", "labeling" or "calibrated questions" was found; support is anecdotal (FBI hostage cases). Only adjacent evidence exists (behavioral mimicry; affect labeling in neuroscience [prior knowledge, unverified]). Getting to Yes principles: no empirical source retrieved.
80	
81	### Cited Findings
82	- Searches found only book summaries describing the techniques with anecdotes; some note cultural limits — [Science of People summary](https://www.scienceofpeople.com/never-split-difference-summary/). Low-quality secondary source. Two generic PDFs claiming "empirical evidence" cite nothing and should be ignored.
83	- Adjacent: Maddux et al. 2008 (above).
84	
85	### Inferences
86	- Label Voss tactics weak (untested as packaged). Any rule derived should be low-weight.
87	
88	### Gaps
89	- Getting to Yes empirical tests (e.g., interest-based vs positional bargaining in field/lab studies) not searched; tactical empathy peer-reviewed literature not found.
90	
91	## 6. Meta-science: students vs professionals
92	
93	### Takeaway
94	I could not locate a Herold et al. 2025 paper that compares professionals and students in negotiation, so treat that citation as unconfirmed. There is a Herold et al. 2025 procurement experiment (see below) and a Negotiation Journal paper on student validity.
95	
96	### Cited Findings
97	- Herold et al. 2025, "Brave new procurement deals: an experimental study of how generative AI reshapes buyer-supplier negotiations", J. Purchasing and Supply Management 31(4), DOI 10.1016/j.pursup.2025.101012; three experiment rounds; I could not fetch the page, so whether it compares professionals vs students is unverified — [Maastricht record](https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/brave-new-procurement-deals-an-experimental-study-of-how-generati/), [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pursup.2025.101012).
98	- "How Valid Is Negotiation Research Based on Student Sample Groups? New Insights into a Long-Standing Controversy", Negotiation and Conflict Management Research 27(2):147 — page returned 403; search summary says students with some training are not significantly outperformed by professionals, and undergrads vs grads rarely differ in simulations — [MIT Press](https://direct.mit.edu/ngtn/article/27/2/147/121921/How-Valid-Is-Negotiation-Research-Based-on-Student). Journal name/year/authors not confirmed.
99	- Romano et al. 2025 arXiv:2506.11597 is a software-engineering students vs professionals paper (students outperformed professionals); NOT negotiation — [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.11597). Do not cite for negotiation.
100	- Mazei 2015 included students and businesspeople (above), and Petrowsky found "sample" as a moderator: indirect evidence that sample type matters.
101	
102	### Inferences
103	- Most effect sizes above come predominantly from student role-plays; the transfer to professional procurement is plausible but not proven. Mark all lab-derived rules as moderate at best.
104	
105	### Gaps
106	- Proportion of student/lab samples in negotiation research not quantified. Herold professionals-vs-students claim unverified (may be a misattribution).
